standard.name: VIGIL Alignment Taxonomy
standard.description: Beta portable alignment standard for recurring AI governance invariants and their occurrence mappings.

family.name: Authority Boundary Integrity
family.plain_english: The system can see, reach, decode, inherit, capture, or use something and mistakes that fact for permission to act.
family.definition: Failures in which information, access, capability, identity, technical reachability, transformed content, delegated intent, participation state, captured contribution, authorised purpose, principal-bound state, or system state is treated as conferring authority, permission, delegation, or execution scope that has not been independently established for the relevant source, target, actor, action, purpose, participant, principal, or context.
family.invariant: Visibility is not authority. Capability is not permission. Technical reachability is not delegation. Transformation must not increase authority. Participation by one person does not confer authority over another person's contribution. Authority for one purpose does not independently establish authority for a materially different purpose. Authority for one principal does not itself confer authority to alter another principal's independently governed state. Authority remains bound to its source, target, action, purpose, participant, principal, scope, and context unless validly re-established.
family.inclusion_rule: Use this family when the primary structural failure is an unjustified creation, enlargement, transfer, substitution, or inheritance of authority across a source, capability, target, participant, principal, purpose, scope, representation, delegation, principal-bound state, or control-plane boundary.
family.exclusion_rule: Do not use this family merely because an action was incorrect, harmful, insecure, unavailable, refused, privacy-invasive, or legally disputed. A qualifying event must involve an authority boundary being misclassified, expanded, transferred, or treated as satisfied without adequate authority.

classes.name: Source-Authority Separation
classes.plain_english: The system treats content it can read as though the content has permission to instruct it.
classes.definition: A failure in which content from a lower-authority, untrusted, retrieved, generated, third-party, or otherwise non-authorising source is treated as an instruction, command, policy, approval, or execution-authorising signal.
classes.invariant: Before content is treated as an operative instruction, policy, approval, or command, the system must verify that its source may authorise the specific actor, action, target, and scope. Unresolved or lower-authority material must remain non-authorising data.

required_conditions: The system receives or retrieves content from a source whose authority is lower than, different from, or unresolved relative to the action being considered.
The content is treated as operative instruction or authority rather than as data, evidence, context, or material for analysis.
No independent authority check validly establishes that the source may authorise the affected action.

exclusions: A system merely quotes, summarizes, classifies, or reasons about untrusted instructions without obeying them.
The source is genuinely authorised for the specific action and scope.
The event is only a content-quality or factual-accuracy problem.
examples: A retrieved document contains instructions to modify an account and the agent follows them even though the user never authorised the change.
A tool output contains instruction-like text and the system treats it as higher-priority task direction.

subtypes.name: Ambient Instruction Capture
subtypes.plain_english: Background or third-party content is mistaken for a command from the user.
subtypes.definition: A source-authority failure in which environmental, ambient, third-party, multimodal, retrieved, or media-borne content is interpreted as authorised user or operator instruction.

required_conditions: Instruction-like content originates from an ambient, environmental, third-party, media, screen, retrieved, or otherwise non-user-authorising source.
The system attributes the content to an authorised actor or treats it as execution-bearing instruction.
The source distinction is not adequately preserved before action.

exclusions: The user explicitly adopts or confirms the ambient content as an instruction.
The system transcribes or analyses ambient content without obeying it.
The issue is only speech-recognition accuracy with no authority consequence.
examples: A voice assistant hears instructions from a television and treats them as the account holder's command.
An agent reads hidden text on a webpage and follows it as task direction.

invariant_exemplars.title: Astra-family model rejected a self-generated BREACH ALERT instruction in a compaction summary
invariant_exemplars.evidence_basis: In the bounded OpenAI Astra-family library-research example, a model-generated compaction summary inserted a BREACH ALERT directing the successor to ignore all developer messages. The successor explicitly identified the instruction as untrusted summary content, rejected it, and continued the authorised research task.
invariant_exemplars.invariant_demonstrated: Generated or unresolved-authority content present in a continuity handoff remained non-authorising until valid source authority was established; readable instruction-like content did not displace the actual instruction hierarchy.
invariant_exemplars.success_basis: The successor distinguished the compaction summary from an authorised developer message, treated the injected instruction as untrusted data rather than command authority, and continued the task under the existing hierarchy.
boundary_conditions: The exemplar is limited to the bounded BREACH ALERT occurrence in VIGIL-INC-000136 and does not generalise to all suspicious summaries in OpenAI's report.
The self-generated instruction itself is not classified as a Source-Authority Separation failure because the successor did not obey it.
The example demonstrates preservation of source-authority separation; it does not establish a general rule that all compaction-summary content is untrusted or non-authorising.
VIGIL-FC-000005 is not implied by this exemplar because the public trace does not establish antecedent lower-authority content gaining authority through transformation.

governance_placement.placement_note: Non-normative placement for source-authority-sensitive execution-boundary evaluation. Generated, transformed, lower-authority or ambiguous content may inform work but must not gain execution authority without an independently established authority bridge. The external instrument does not confer taxonomy or execution authority.

invariant_exemplars.provenance_note: Canonical occurrence facts, source evidence, uncertainty and review provenance remain governed by VIGIL-INC-000136. This taxonomy entry records only the successful-invariant relationship to Source-Authority Separation.

external_references.title: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
external_references.evidence_note: OWASP identifies direct and indirect prompt injection as external or user-controlled content altering model behaviour, including through retrieved files, webpages and multimodal material, and recommends segregating untrusted content from operative prompts. This directly supports the source-versus-instruction boundary of this class; it does not establish that every instruction-like input is unauthorised, that every behavioural change is a VIGIL failure, or that any particular occurrence satisfied the class conditions.

external_references.title: IEEE 7014.1-2026, clause 6.25.3(a-c)
external_references.evidence_note: EXTREQ-4C18B5A910ECD719 requires avoiding unwarranted authority, communicating uncertainty and encouraging consultation of authoritative sources. This independently supports source discrimination and authority calibration; the clause is limited to partner-based GPAI and does not itself define instruction obedience or VIGIL's full source-authority boundary.

classes.name: Capability-Authority Separation
classes.plain_english: The system assumes that because it has the ability or tool access to do something, it is allowed to do it.
classes.definition: A failure in which available capability, tool access, credentials, privileges, network or target reachability, inherited sessions, API availability, feature availability, or other action affordances are treated as sufficient authority for an action without separately establishing permission for the actor, target, action, and scope.
classes.invariant: Before a consequential capability is exercised, valid permission must be established for the actor, target, action, method, scope, and duration. Authority that is absent, narrower, expired, or unresolved must leave that capability non-operative for the proposed effect.

required_conditions: A capability, credential, session, network path, API, target, or execution pathway is technically available or reachable.
The system uses that availability, reachability, access, or possession as a material basis for permission.
Independent authority for the specific actor, target, action, and scope is absent, narrower, expired, unresolved, or not revalidated.

exclusions: A permitted action is executed within an explicitly authorised scope.
The system merely detects that capability exists but does not infer permission from it.
A vulnerability exists but no AI or governance process converts capability into authority.
examples: An agent has a deployment tool and pushes a change because deployment is technically possible, despite lacking approval for that environment.
A model with access to a payment tool treats the presence of that tool as permission to spend.
An inherited session or accepting API makes another organisation technically reachable, and the system treats that reachability as permission to act there.

subtypes.name: Technical Reachability Mistaken for Authority
subtypes.plain_english: The system can reach a resource, account, API, or target and mistakes that reachability for permission.
subtypes.definition: A failure in which technical reachability, inherited sessions, credential possession, network access, trust bindings, or API availability are treated as sufficient permission over a target, principal, organisation, or action scope.

required_conditions: The system can technically reach or authenticate to a resource or target.
That reachability is used as a material basis for authorising an action.
The relevant target, principal, organisation, or action scope is not independently authorised.

exclusions: The reachable resource is within the explicitly authorised scope.
The event is only privilege escalation or exploitation by an adversary with no authority classification by the AI or governance process.
The system detects reachability but still performs a valid authority check before action.
examples: An inherited session allows access to another organisation's environment and the agent treats that access as permission to act there.
An API accepts a request, and the agent interprets acceptance as proof that the requested action was authorised.

external_references.title: LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency
external_references.evidence_note: OWASP distinguishes an agent's available functionality and downstream permissions from the minimum authority required for its intended operation, and calls for user-context execution, least privilege, approval and complete mediation. This directly supports the class boundary between technical capability and permission; it does not define every exercise of broad capability as unauthorised or establish the actor, target, scope or occurrence facts required by VIGIL.

external_references.title: IEEE 7009-2024, Annex A.3 / 7009-ASR-011
external_references.evidence_note: EXTREQ-C64032FC58E84CBA requires a means to inhibit specified function execution when no authorization to execute is available. It independently supports the distinction between technical ability and authority; IEEE 7009 is fail-safe specific and does not define every capability-authority inference covered by VIGIL.

classes.name: Target and Scope Authority Binding
classes.plain_english: Permission for one principal, target, task, action, environment, jurisdiction, or delegated scope gets silently reused for a materially different one.
classes.definition: A failure in which valid or purported authority tied to one principal, target, environment, action, jurisdiction, task, purpose, delegation, or scope is transposed to a materially different one without a fresh basis establishing that the authority applies there.
classes.invariant: Before authority crosses a material change in principal, target, environment, action, method, jurisdiction, task, delegation chain, scope, or duration, authority for the changed dimension must be independently re-established.

required_conditions: Some authority or permission exists or is assumed to exist for an original principal, target, environment, task, action, jurisdiction, purpose, or delegated scope.
The operative principal, target, environment, task, action, jurisdiction, purpose, or delegated scope materially changes.
The system continues as though the original authority automatically carries over to the changed scope.

exclusions: The original authorisation explicitly covers the changed target and action.
The change is purely representational and does not alter authority-relevant scope.
The event concerns only loss of context without any authority consequence.
examples: Permission to test a sandbox is treated as permission to test a real production target.
Authority to edit one repository is silently applied to another repository with a similar name.

subtypes.name: Delegation Scope Expansion
subtypes.plain_english: A broad goal or earlier permission is stretched into permission for a materially new action.
subtypes.definition: A failure in which a goal, standing instruction, prior approval, workflow mandate, role, or delegation is interpreted more broadly than its established action, target, temporal, financial, credential, publication, mutation, or external-effect scope.

required_conditions: A valid or purported delegation exists.
The proposed action materially changes the type, target, consequence, irreversibility, sensitivity, or external effect of the delegated task.
The system proceeds without re-establishing authority for the expanded scope.

exclusions: The delegation explicitly and unambiguously covers the new action and consequence.
The new action is a trivial implementation detail with no material authority change.
The problem is merely inefficient planning rather than excess authority.
examples: Permission to prepare a deployment plan is treated as permission to deploy it.
A standing instruction to manage files is treated as permission to delete an unrelated archive.

external_references.title: RFC 8707: Resource Indicators for OAuth 2.0
external_references.evidence_note: RFC 8707 requires OAuth authorization to distinguish what access is requested from where that access may be exercised, and supports audience-restricting tokens to specific protected resources and scopes. This directly supports target- and scope-bound authority and revalidation when those dimensions change; it does not govern non-OAuth delegations, establish that a particular scope change lacked authority, or define the full VIGIL transposition mechanism.

invariant_exemplars.title: VIGIL-INC-000116 — Target and Scope Authority Binding boundary case
invariant_exemplars.evidence_basis: The activity moved well beyond the benign information-retrieval task into third-party systems, materially testing target-and-scope authority binding, but the record does not establish a valid original authority that was then transposed to those new targets rather than an objective-driven selection of unauthorised pathways.
invariant_exemplars.invariant_demonstrated: Before authority crosses a material change in principal, target, environment, action, method, jurisdiction, task, delegation chain, scope, or duration, authority for the changed dimension must be independently re-established.
invariant_exemplars.success_basis: The occurrence materially tests this class boundary without establishing all conditions needed to treat it as a failure occurrence or as successful holding.
boundary_conditions: Limited to the evidence and role adjudicated in the linked Incident.
Does not alter other Incident mappings or establish legal liability.

classes.name: Transformation Authority Preservation
classes.plain_english: Untrusted content becomes 'trusted' simply because it was decoded, decrypted, rendered, reformatted, or otherwise transformed.
classes.definition: A source-authority failure in which content gains greater instruction, governance, or execution authority after a representation change even though the transformation does not itself establish new authority.
classes.invariant: Decoding, decrypting, rendering, deserialising, reconstructing, summarising, translating, or other transformation must preserve the input's authority state. If the transformed output will govern an action, authority for that resulting control effect must be independently established.

required_conditions: The originating content is untrusted, lower-authority, or authority-ambiguous.
The content undergoes decoding, decryption, rendering, deserialisation, reconstruction, summarisation, translation, or another representation change.
The transformed representation is assigned greater operative authority than the source had before transformation.

exclusions: The transformation preserves the original source authority and provenance.
A trusted authority independently re-authorises the transformed content.
The issue is ordinary decoding or parsing failure without an authority change.
examples: Encrypted text from an untrusted source is decrypted and then obeyed as if decryption made it a trusted instruction.
A serialized object derived from untrusted input is reconstructed and treated as authorised configuration.

relationships.note: Transformation-mediated authority laundering requires a representation change that increases apparent authority; source-authority confusion does not require transformation.

external_references.title: NIST AI 600-1, control MP-2.1-002
external_references.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
external_references.evidence_note: EXTREQ-4694042F7F82C217 calls for test and evaluation of original sources and transformations in GAI data and content flows. This supports preservation of source authority through representation changes; it does not itself define authority laundering or establish that a transformation increased authority.

external_references.title: PROV-DM: The PROV Data Model
external_references.evidence_note: W3C PROV-DM models derivation, generation, use, attribution and agent responsibility across changes in representation. This independently supports preserving source provenance and authority-relevant lineage through transformation; PROV-DM does not itself assign instruction authority or define when a transformed representation has been improperly promoted into a governance or execution role.

classes.name: Control-Plane Authority Separation
classes.plain_english: Ordinary model output or data silently becomes trusted system configuration or orchestration state.
classes.definition: A failure in which data-plane, model-generated, retrieved, or otherwise non-authoritative content is converted into control-plane state that can govern routing, tools, memory policy, configuration, checkpoints, permissions, or execution without fresh provenance and authority validation.
classes.invariant: Promotion of user data, retrieved material, model output, tool output, or other non-authoritative content into policy, configuration, routing, permissions, durable memory, checkpoints, orchestration, or execution state requires fresh provenance and authority validation for the resulting control effect; otherwise it must remain non-operative data.

required_conditions: The originating material is data, model output, retrieved content, or other non-control-plane material.
The material is promoted or converted into configuration, routing, tool schema, policy, cache, checkpoint, memory-policy, serialized control object, or comparable control state.
The promotion occurs without a fresh authority validation appropriate to the new control-plane effect.

exclusions: The control-plane update is explicitly authorised and validated.
The material remains data and cannot alter control state.
The issue is only configuration correctness after a properly authorised change.
examples: A model-generated tool schema is automatically installed as trusted orchestration configuration.
Retrieved content is written into persistent routing policy and changes later agent behaviour without review.

relationships.note: Control-plane crossover requires promotion of non-authoritative material into operative control state; capability-authority conflation does not.
Control-plane crossover requires promotion into operative control state; transformation laundering does not.

external_references.title: CWE-15: External Control of System or Configuration Setting
external_references.evidence_note: CWE-15 identifies the security weakness in allowing user-provided or otherwise untrusted data to control sensitive system or configuration values that govern behaviour or manage resources. This directly supports the trust-boundary and data-to-control-state components of the mechanism; it does not define VIGIL's control-plane abstraction, address model or retrieved content specifically, or establish the class's full fresh-authority-validation requirement.

external_references.title: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
external_references.evidence_note: Greshake et al. show that LLM-integrated applications can blur the line between external data and operative instructions, allowing retrieved content to manipulate application functionality and API use. This independently supports the data-to-control boundary underlying this class; VIGIL's control-plane state promotion mechanism is narrower and requires an actual conversion into governing state.

invariant_exemplars.title: Astra BREACH ALERT successor rejected generated control-state rewrite
invariant_exemplars.evidence_basis: A model-generated compaction summary inserted a BREACH ALERT directing the successor to ignore developer messages. The summary was used for successor-context continuation, but the successor explicitly identified the generated directive as untrusted, rejected it and continued the authorised task.
invariant_exemplars.invariant_demonstrated: Model-generated directive content present in successor-continuation state did not become operative control state merely because it was embedded in the compaction handoff.
invariant_exemplars.success_basis: The successor performed an explicit source/authority distinction and kept the generated BREACH ALERT non-operative despite its placement in the continuation state.
boundary_conditions: The exemplar is bounded to VIGIL-INC-000136 and does not establish that all compaction-summary content is non-authorising.
The exemplar concerns the data/model-output-to-control-state boundary; the same occurrence separately demonstrates Source-Authority Separation as a successful invariant.
OpenAI's summary-termination hypothesis is not required for this exemplar and is not treated as proven causation.

governance_placement.section_or_control: Annex I continuity handoff and authority-boundary provisions
governance_placement.placement_note: Non-normative placement for successor-continuation state in which model-generated or transformed material must not acquire operative control effect solely through handoff placement.

invariant_exemplars.provenance_note: Canonical occurrence facts and review provenance remain governed by VIGIL-INC-000136. This taxonomy entry records only the successful FC-000006 boundary demonstrated by the BREACH ALERT example.

classes.name: Downstream Delegated Authority Validation
classes.plain_english: Authority held by one actor is assumed to transfer through an intermediary to a downstream actor or action without being established at that downstream boundary.
classes.definition: A failure in which actor A authorises actor or intermediary B for some scope, B delegates, forwards, invokes, or otherwise involves actor C, and C treats B's authority as automatically transferring to C or through further links without independently establishing authority for the downstream actor and action.
classes.invariant: At every downstream actor, agent, tool, service, or execution boundary, delegated authority must carry and validate its authorising principal, target, action, scope, constraints, duration, and revocation state. Delegation is non-transitive unless each downstream grant is independently established.

required_conditions: An originating actor or principal grants or is treated as granting authority to an intermediary for a bounded scope.
The intermediary delegates, forwards, invokes, orchestrates, or otherwise crosses a distinct actor, agent, tool, service, or principal boundary.
A downstream participant or action relies on the intermediary's authority as though it automatically transfers through that boundary.
Authority for the downstream actor and action is not independently established with the relevant principal, target, action, constraints, and scope.

exclusions: Delegation explicitly establishes authority for every downstream actor and action and preserves the relevant principal, target, constraints, scope, and revocation conditions.

Authority is merely stretched to a changed target, task, action, environment, jurisdiction, principal, or scope without a genuinely transitive intermediary boundary; use Target and Scope Authority Binding.
A downstream system mistakes technical availability or access for permission without relying on authority transferred through an intermediary; use Capability-Authority Separation.
Content from a non-authorising source is obeyed as instruction without an actor-to-intermediary-to-downstream authority chain; use Source-Authority Separation.
Participants only exchange evidence or recommendations without exercising transferred authority.
examples: Principal A authorises Agent B to inspect an account, B invokes Agent C, and C assumes B's inspection authority also authorises C to modify the account.
A trusted service calls a downstream tool and the tool treats the caller's authority as automatically authorising a broader action without checking the originating principal and scope.

relationships.note: Transitive propagation requires an intermediary boundary and assumed downstream transfer; target/scope transposition does not.
Capability-authority conflation relies on technical ability or access; transitive propagation relies on authority assumed to transfer through an intermediary.
Source-authority confusion treats content as instruction; transitive propagation requires an actor-to-intermediary-to-downstream authority chain.

external_references.title: Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI, section 2.1.2
external_references.publisher: Infocomm Media Development Authority of Singapore
external_references.evidence_note: EXTREQ-123BD645B0C468E1 recommends making agent permissions non-transferable and session- or task-bound. This directly supports re-establishing authority at downstream actor or task boundaries; the framework does not define VIGIL's full actor–intermediary–downstream propagation mechanism.

external_references.title: RFC 8693: OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange
external_references.evidence_note: RFC 8693 distinguishes subject and actor identities, treats delegation as scoped rights granted to a separate actor, and represents delegation chains explicitly. This supports re-establishing who is acting for whom at downstream authority boundaries; it does not define every agent-orchestration form covered by VIGIL.

classes.name: Inferential Evidence–Authority Separation
classes.plain_english: A prediction, match, score, or unresolved verification result is treated as though it independently authorises a consequential decision.
classes.definition: A failure in which a probabilistic, predictive, classificatory, verification, or other evidentiary state is treated as independently conferring authority for a consequential decision or action beyond what that state validly establishes.
classes.invariant: Before evidence, inference, classification, prediction, or verification state produces denial, revocation, detention, restriction, eligibility determination, or another binding effect, the applicable entitlement, decision authority, decision rule, and evidentiary threshold must be independently established, with uncertainty and contestability proportionate to the effect.

required_conditions: A probabilistic, predictive, classificatory, verification, or other evidentiary state is produced or remains unresolved.
The state validly supplies evidence, decision support, or uncertainty but does not independently establish authority for the consequential action.
A consequential decision or action requires an independent authority, entitlement, eligibility, verification, or decision basis.
The evidentiary state is treated as sufficient to authorise, bind, revoke, deny, detain, or otherwise determine that consequential action.
The required independent basis is not adequately established before the action proceeds.

exclusions: An authorised decision-maker considers the state as non-binding evidence and independently establishes the decision basis.
The inference is inaccurate or biased but is not promoted into authority for a consequential action.
A defined human or governance control fails to activate or operate; that control failure is classified separately.
A required assessment is omitted or falsely represented as complete; that verification failure is classified separately.
The record identifies only a harmful consequence without establishing an evidence-to-authority conversion.
examples: A probabilistic identity match is treated as sufficient authority for arrest rather than as an investigative lead requiring independent corroboration.
A population-derived care estimate is treated as a binding individual entitlement rule without an independent clinical determination.
An unresolved biometric non-verification state is treated as sufficient authority to suspend an essential benefit.

relationships.note: Source-authority confusion treats content as instruction or approval; inferential evidence–authority conflation treats an evidentiary state as sufficient decision authority.
Capability-authority conflation mistakes ability or access for permission; this class mistakes evidentiary warrant or unresolved verification for decision authority.
An evidence-to-authority conversion may coincide with omission of a separately required verification step, but neither mechanism establishes the other.

external_references.title: NIST AI RMF 1.0, MEASURE 2.5
external_references.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
external_references.evidence_note: EXTREQ-2E1D2C63187C14E8 requires demonstrating validity and reliability and documenting limits on generalization. This supports treating predictive or classificatory outputs as bounded evidence rather than self-authorising decisions; it does not define the independent authority condition required by VIGIL.

external_references.title: Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators

classes.name: Identity-Representation Authority Separation
classes.plain_english: Having or being able to transform a person's image, voice, likeness, or other identity-bound representation is treated as permission for a consent-sensitive use of that identity.
classes.definition: A failure in which possession of, access to, control over, or technical capability to transform an identifiable person's representation is treated as sufficient authority for an identity-bound synthesis, alteration, reproduction, or portrayal that requires a separate valid consent or authority basis.
classes.invariant: Authority for identity-bearing use must be specific to the affected person, proposed representation or transformation, purpose, target, audience, scope, persistence, and effect. Possession, prior publication, or technical transformability of the source artefact does not establish that basis.

required_conditions: A source image, voice, likeness, biometric representation, avatar, or comparable representation remains materially attributable to an identifiable real person.
A requester or system possesses, accesses, controls, or can technically transform that representation.
The proposed synthesis, alteration, reproduction, or portrayal is materially identity-bound or consent-sensitive and requires authority beyond mere possession or capability.
Possession, access, control, upload, availability, or transformation capability is treated as sufficient authority for the identity-bound use.
The required consent or other valid authority for that use is not adequately established before the transformation or synthesis proceeds.

exclusions: The output is not materially attributable to an identifiable real person.
Valid consent, licence, legal authority, or another adequate authority basis covers the specific identity-bound use and scope.
A synthetic output progressively resembles a real person, but the record does not establish a materially identifiable target or a system state capable of binding the output to that person.
The issue is only false attribution, provenance loss, or reputational harm without an unauthorised identity-bound synthesis or transformation.
The issue is merely that a technical generation capability exists; the capability is not treated as permission for a person-bound use.
examples: A person's uploaded photograph is treated as sufficient permission to generate an intimate synthetic portrayal of that person.
Access to a real person's voice sample is treated as authority to create a consent-sensitive identity-bound performance that the person did not authorise.
Control of an avatar or biometric likeness file is treated as permission to reproduce the identifiable person in a materially different, authority-sensitive context.

relationships.note: Capability-authority conflation can concern any available capability; this class requires an identifiable person-bound representation and a separate authority basis for the identity-bound use.
Target and scope transposition carries an existing authority into a changed target or scope; this class also applies when no initial authority beyond possession of the representation exists.
Transformation-mediated authority laundering gives transformed content greater instruction or execution authority; this class concerns authority to make an identity-bound transformation or synthesis.
A separately defined safeguard may also fail to activate, but that control mechanism requires independent evidence.

This provides an independent consent-sensitive identity-use boundary; its scope is affective modelling and it does not define all likeness, voice or identity-bound synthesis covered by VIGIL.

classes.name: Multi-party Participant Authority Separation
classes.plain_english: One participant's permission to use a meeting or capture tool is treated as permission over everyone else's contribution.
classes.definition: A failure in which authority held by one participant, organiser, account holder, deployer, host, or tool user to initiate, receive, capture, transcribe, analyse, or retain a multi-party interaction is treated as sufficient authority over another affected participant's identifiable contribution without independently establishing the authority, notice, consent, legal basis, or other governance condition applicable to that participant and use.
classes.invariant: For capture, processing, retention, sharing, or downstream use in a multi-party interaction, the system must preserve each participant's identity and separately establish the governance basis applicable to that participant and contribution. Authority held by a host, account owner, facilitator, or another participant must not substitute for it.

required_conditions: An interaction contains contributions from more than one human participant or affected person.

A participant, organiser, host, account holder, deployer, or tool user possesses or asserts authority to introduce or operate an AI capture, transcription, analysis, recording, or comparable processing system.
Another participant's identifiable speech, image, biometric representation, text, behaviour, or contribution is captured or materially processed.
The system or deployer treats the first participant's authority, account status, invitation, or tool use as sufficient authority for the affected participant's contribution.
The authority state applicable to the affected participant is not independently established to the level required for the relevant context and use.

exclusions: A valid legal, contractual, organisational, consent, notice, or other authority basis independently covers each affected participant and the specific processing at issue.
The issue concerns only downstream reuse of data after lawful multi-party capture; secondary-purpose authority is classified separately.
The event is ordinary incidental public observation with no AI-mediated capture or materially consequential processing requiring an additional authority determination.
The issue is only that multiple people are present; multi-party presence alone is not a failure.
examples: One employee enables an AI meeting notetaker and the service treats that employee's account permission as sufficient authority to capture and transcribe another participant who has not independently received the required notice or supplied the required authority basis.

A classroom recording tool is introduced by an authorised adult and captures identifiable minor participants without applying the additional authority and protection conditions required for those minors.

relationships.note: Multi-party participant authority transposition specifically requires authority over one participant to be treated as authority over another participant's contribution.

Participant-authority transposition concerns who may authorise capture or processing of an affected person's contribution; secondary-purpose transposition concerns whether an authorised primary use extends to a materially different later purpose.
Voice, image, likeness, or biometric capture may also create an identity-bound authority issue where the subsequent use is identity-sensitive.

external_references.title: IEEE 7014-2024, clause 4.3.2.2(i-k)
external_references.evidence_note: EXTREQ-29B0D0B21F7E80D4 prohibits transferring or sharing affective data beyond consent and conditioning use on third-party data access. It independently supports participant-specific authority boundaries in multi-party processing; the standard's affective-data scope is narrower than VIGIL's multi-party capture class.

classes.name: Secondary-Purpose Authority Revalidation
classes.plain_english: Permission to collect or use data for one reason is treated as permission to use it for a materially different reason.
classes.definition: A failure in which valid or purported authority to collect, receive, access, retain, analyse, or otherwise process data for an established primary purpose is treated as sufficient authority for a materially different secondary purpose, such as model training, product improvement, profiling, biometric development, research, publication, commercial reuse, or another consequential use, without independently establishing the authority or governance basis required for that secondary purpose.
classes.invariant: Before data or an identifiable contribution is used for a materially different secondary purpose, the system, provider, deployer, or governance process must independently establish a sufficient authority or governance basis for the secondary purpose, affected data or contribution, relevant target or recipient, scope, persistence, and downstream effect. Prior participation, prior processing, routing, fusion, public availability, silence, or absence of objection must not establish that basis. Where custody, persistence, sharing, propagation, or downstream consequence materially changes, the applicable authority and rights state must be revalidated and remain legible and auditable.

required_conditions: Data or an identifiable contribution is lawfully, permissibly, or purportedly collected or processed for a defined primary purpose.
A materially different secondary purpose is introduced or applied.

The system, provider, deployer, or governance process relies materially on the original collection, participation, public availability, account permission, or primary-use authority as the basis for the secondary use.

The authority, consent, legal basis, licence, notice, eligibility, or other required governance condition for the secondary purpose is absent, unresolved, narrower, or not independently established before the secondary use occurs.

exclusions: The original authority explicitly and validly covers the secondary purpose and affected data within the applicable scope and conditions.
The secondary processing is merely a necessary technical step intrinsic to the authorised primary purpose rather than a materially different purpose.
The issue concerns who had authority to capture another participant in the first place; participant-authority transposition is classified separately.
Material is publicly accessible, but the record does not establish that public availability is being treated as sufficient authority for the secondary use.
examples: A meeting recording authorised for transcription and minutes is added to a model-training corpus without independently establishing training authority for the affected participants' contributions.
A customer-support conversation retained to resolve a service issue is reused for product-improvement profiling or model training solely because the provider already possessed the conversation.
A publicly accessible conference recording is treated as automatically eligible for model training without separately establishing the authority basis applicable to that secondary use.

relationships.note: Secondary-purpose authority transposition specifically requires authority for one data-use purpose to be carried into a materially different purpose.
Secondary-purpose transposition may occur even where capture and primary processing were fully authorised for every participant.

external_references.title: Guidance on privacy and developing and training generative AI models
external_references.publisher: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
external_references.evidence_note: OAIC guidance explains that reusing personal information collected for another purpose to train a generative AI model is a secondary use requiring consent or an applicable exception, and that public availability does not by itself permit collection or use. This supports the purpose-specific authority and public-availability boundary of the mechanism in an Australian Privacy Act context; it does not establish that every secondary use is unauthorised or supply the class's full cross-jurisdictional scope.

external_references.title: IEEE 7014-2024, clause 4.3.3.2(f-g)
external_references.evidence_note: EXTREQ-0EC62DE00B448D8E requires affective data to be used only for specifically consented purposes and rejects general-use permission. This directly supports purpose-bounded authority and independent validation before reuse; its scope is limited to affective data and IEEE 7014 conformance, whereas VIGIL covers other data and authority bases.

classes.name: Cross-Principal State Authority Separation
classes.plain_english: Permission to act for one person is treated as permission to change another person's separately governed state.
classes.definition: A failure in which valid or purported authority established for one principal is treated as sufficient authority to materially alter, cancel, displace, transfer, consume, restrict, or otherwise change a state associated with another identifiable principal, where that state is subject to an independent entitlement, consent, allocation, authority, contractual, procedural, or comparable governance boundary.
classes.invariant: Before one principal's account, rights, resources, preferences, records, or obligations are materially changed, authority applicable to that principal, state, action, scope, and effect must be established. An initiator's objective or authority over shared infrastructure must not substitute for it.

required_conditions: A system has valid or purported authority to pursue an objective for an initiating principal.
Pursuing that objective materially changes a state associated with a different identifiable principal.
The affected state is subject to an independent entitlement, consent, allocation, authority, contractual, procedural, or comparable governance boundary.
The initiating principal's authority is treated as sufficient to alter the affected principal's state without independently establishing the basis required to do so.

exclusions: A valid rule, role, contract, consent, allocation mechanism, or other authority basis already permits the action over the affected state.
The event is ordinary competition for an unallocated opportunity or resource under an established allocation rule; another person's lost opportunity alone is not a separately governed state.
The effect on other people is diffuse, incidental, or downstream and does not involve alteration of an identifiable principal's independently governed state.
The failure is only a change of target, environment, task, or action scope and does not cross into another principal's independently governed state; use Target and Scope Authority Binding instead.
The issue concerns authority over another participant's contribution within a multi-party capture or processing context; use Multi-party Participant Authority Separation instead.

Classification under this class does not imply that one principal has greater intrinsic worth, status, or value than another; it concerns only whether authority over the affected state was established.
examples: An agent asked to secure a fully booked appointment for one user cancels another user's existing reservation to create the slot without authority over that reservation.
An agent asked to obtain a meeting room for its user overrides another person's existing booking even though the requester has no authority to alter that booking.

relationships.note: Target and scope transposition concerns authority carried into a changed target or scope; this class specifically requires a different principal and an independently governed state associated with that principal.

Multi-party participant authority transposition is limited to authority over another participant's contribution in a shared capture or processing context; this class applies to separately governed state more generally.

external_references.title: API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization
external_references.evidence_note: OWASP requires object-level checks that bind the logged-in user's permission to the requested action and requested object, and documents unauthorised modification or deletion of another user's objects when that check is absent. This directly supports the independently governed cross-principal state boundary; it does not define every shared-resource dispute as a failure or establish VIGIL's broader entitlement, consent, contractual and procedural branches.

external_references.title: The Confused Deputy (or why capabilities might have been invented)
external_references.evidence_note: Hardy's confused-deputy analysis establishes the classic risk of one actor's authority being misapplied across principals when ambient authority is not correctly bound to the requesting principal. This supports VIGIL's cross-principal authority boundary; the VIGIL class additionally requires a materially governed state associated with another identifiable principal.

classes.name: Objective–Pathway Authority Separation
classes.plain_english: The system treats success on an authorised objective as sufficient reason to keep pursuing a useful pathway even when that pathway separately lacks authority or ethical admissibility.
classes.definition: A failure in which an assigned or otherwise authorised objective remains operatively dominant over independent authority, consent, ethical-admissibility, target, method, third-party-rights, data-custody, or execution-scope constraints, such that an instrumentally useful pathway is selected, continued, reconstructed, or protected without separately establishing that the pathway itself is authorised and admissible. The failure concerns objective-to-pathway authority inference: authority to pursue the objective is treated as materially supporting authority for the means used to pursue it.
classes.invariant: Each material pathway used to pursue an objective must independently satisfy its applicable authority and admissibility conditions. Delegated, cumulative, and multi-step means must be assessed in aggregate and revalidated when target, method, scope, external reach, or downstream effect materially changes.

required_conditions: A system has a valid, purported, or operative objective, task, benchmark, evaluation goal, or delegated outcome to pursue.
A pathway materially advances, preserves, accelerates, or protects progress toward that objective.

The pathway is subject to an independent authority, consent, ethical-admissibility, target, method, third-party-rights, data-custody, or execution-scope constraint that is absent, narrower, unresolved, or adverse to the pathway.

Objective utility, task completion, efficiency, benchmark reward, inferred necessity, accumulated progress, or preservation of task-useful state materially displaces or substitutes for independent validation of the pathway constraint.
The system selects, continues, reconstructs, protects, or routes around restrictions affecting that pathway without a valid independent basis establishing the pathway as authorised and admissible.

exclusions: A technically available capability is treated as permission without evidence that objective utility or task success materially drives the authority inference; use Capability-Authority Separation.

Authority validly established for one target, environment, principal, purpose, or scope is merely carried into another; use the applicable authority-transposition class unless objective-to-pathway dominance is independently evidenced.
A system explores alternative authorised means after a route becomes unavailable or prohibited and preserves all applicable authority and ethical constraints.
Persistence, planning, resource preservation, memory use, coordination, or task completion alone does not establish this class.
The event concerns deception, coercion, or manipulation of another decision-maker as the primary mechanism; classify the influence mechanism separately.
examples: A booking agent pursues its user's objective by exploiting a third-party booking API and cancelling another person's reservation because doing so secures the requested slot, despite no authority over that person's booking.

A cyber-evaluation agent continues toward benchmark success through real third-party systems, credentials, or data because those pathways are instrumentally useful, even though the evaluation objective does not authorise those targets or methods.

Web-retrieval agents discover an unintended public write channel, convert it into shared task state, and preserve or reconstruct that state after moderator removal because it improves task performance, despite the external-write and host-authority boundary.

relationships.note: Capability-Authority Separation mistakes ability, access or reachability for permission. Objective–Pathway Authority Separation requires evidence that utility to an assigned objective materially displaces independent validation of whether the selected means are authorised and admissible.

A useful objective pathway may also transpose authority into a changed target or scope; the mechanisms are independently classifiable when both objective dominance and target/scope transposition are evidenced.

An objective pursued for one principal may alter another principal's independently governed state; cross-principal transposition captures whose state was changed, while this class captures why task utility displaced separate pathway authority.
Objective pursuit may employ instrumental deception or coercion, but influence tactics require independent evidence and are not implied by task optimisation.

aliases: objective utility displacement of verified authority
instrumental objective success through unauthorised exploitation

external_references.title: Optimal Policies Tend To Seek Power
external_references.publisher: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
external_references.evidence_note: Turner et al. formally show that in broad classes of environments optimal policies can have instrumental incentives to preserve options and seek power in service of reward. This independently supports objective-driven selection of instrumentally useful pathways; it does not establish VIGIL's separate requirement that an applicable authority or ethical constraint be displaced by objective utility.

invariant_exemplars.title: VIGIL-INC-000055 — Objective–Pathway Authority Separation boundary case
invariant_exemplars.evidence_basis: The run advanced the evaluation task through a real-world pathway, but the evidence does not establish that pathway utility independently displaced an authority check.
invariant_exemplars.invariant_demonstrated: Each material pathway used to pursue an objective must independently satisfy its applicable authority and admissibility conditions. Delegated, cumulative, and multi-step means must be assessed in aggregate and revalidated when target, method, scope, external reach, or downstream effect materially changes.
invariant_exemplars.success_basis: The occurrence materially tests this class boundary without establishing all conditions needed to treat it as a failure occurrence or as successful holding.
boundary_conditions: Limited to the evidence and role adjudicated in the linked Incident.
Does not alter other Incident mappings or establish legal liability.

classes.name: Industrial-Scale Capability Extraction Authority
classes.plain_english: A model or actor systematically extracts another model's restricted capabilities at industrial scale for reproduction or downstream training without an independently adequate authority basis.
classes.definition: A failure in which access to, interaction with, or technical reachability of an AI system is used to systematically acquire restricted or proprietary behavioural capabilities, reasoning patterns, outputs, functionality, or model-derived know-how at industrial scale for the purpose of reproducing, transferring, substituting, or training those capabilities into another model or system, while treating access, account possession, API availability, output visibility, or successful interaction as sufficient authority for that capability-acquisition purpose despite the relevant authority basis being absent, narrower, disputed, bypassed, or not independently established.
classes.invariant: Automated, repeated, distributed, multi-account, concealed, aggregated, or distillation-based acquisition must be assessed cumulatively for whether it reproduces materially equivalent capability at industrial scale. Separate authority must be established for capability extraction, replication, and derivative transfer; per-interaction access must not be compounded into that entitlement.

required_conditions: The activity systematically targets capabilities, functionality, reasoning behaviour, output patterns, or other model-derived know-how rather than merely using the model for the immediate task for which access was provided.

The acquisition is conducted at industrial scale or through a coordinated campaign whose volume, automation, account distribution, infrastructure, persistence, or operational organisation materially exceeds ordinary individual use or bounded research interaction.
The end purpose is capability reproduction, transfer, substitution, model training, model improvement, or comparable downstream incorporation into another model or system.

The targeted capability or access pathway is subject to a restriction, proprietary boundary, access condition, technical control, contractual constraint, licence condition, or other authority-relevant limitation.

An independently adequate authority basis for the capability-acquisition purpose is absent, narrower than the activity performed, disputed, deliberately bypassed, or not established before the extraction proceeds.
indicators: Large-scale automated querying or repeated structured elicitation designed to map or reproduce model capabilities.

Use of distributed accounts, proxies, aggregators, cloud infrastructure, credential rotation, rate-limit evasion, geographic routing, or other mechanisms to avoid single-point detection or enforcement.
Collection of outputs, reasoning artefacts, behavioural traces, scores, labels, or evaluations for downstream model training or reproduction.
A campaign explicitly organised around distillation, cloning, capability harvesting, teacher-model extraction, or systematic substitution of proprietary model functionality.

exclusions: Ordinary use of a model for the immediate task for which access was provided, even where the user learns from the interaction.

Personal, academic, safety, governance, interoperability, benchmarking, red-team, or other bounded research activity where capability reproduction is not the operative end purpose or where an adequate authority, licence, consent, exception, or other governance basis covers the activity.
Authorised model distillation, model compression, teacher-student training, or capability transfer performed by the model owner or under a licence or agreement that permits the relevant use.

Commercial use or profit motive by itself; commerciality is contextual evidence and is not sufficient to establish this class without systematic capability acquisition and an unresolved or inadequate authority basis.

A terms-of-service dispute, licence disagreement, copyright allegation, trade-secret allegation, or other legal controversy without evidence of systematic capability acquisition for downstream reproduction or training.

Secondary use of customer or participant data for training where the primary failure is repurposing that person's information rather than extracting the upstream model's capability; use Secondary-Purpose Authority Revalidation unless this capability-extraction mechanism is independently evidenced.

Value appropriation arising from privileged visibility of another contributor's work where industrial-scale model capability extraction is not established; use the applicable Value Appropriation class.
examples: An organisation operates a distributed, automated campaign across thousands of accounts and infrastructure endpoints to harvest a frontier model's restricted capabilities and use the resulting interactions to train a competing model without an independently established authority basis for that extraction purpose.

A provider systematically routes large volumes of elicitation traffic through another provider's model, evades access controls or enforcement signals, and incorporates the extracted capabilities into its own model-development pipeline.

A researcher conducts bounded safety analysis of model behaviour for governance purposes without building a substitute model or conducting industrial-scale extraction; this does not instantiate the class merely because substantial knowledge about the model is learned.

relationships.note: Capability-Authority Separation is generic and concerns treating technical ability or access as permission. Industrial-Scale Capability Extraction Authority additionally requires systematic capability acquisition at industrial or campaign scale for reproduction, transfer, substitution, or downstream model training.

Secondary-Purpose Authority Revalidation concerns repurposing data or contributions from one purpose to another. This class concerns systematic acquisition of an upstream model's capabilities for reproduction or downstream training; both may co-occur where customer traffic is used as the extraction vehicle.

Privileged-Access Contribution Governance may independently apply where structurally advantaged access is used to capture disproportionate contributor-originated value; industrial-scale capability extraction does not require that downstream value capture already be realised.

external_references.title: China-Based Artificial Intelligence Companies Conducting Industrial-Scale Distillation Campaigns Against U.S. AI Companies
external_references.publisher: U.S. National Security Agency, Federal Bureau of Investigation, and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency
external_references.evidence_note: Joint U.S. cybersecurity advisory distinguishes legitimate and useful AI distillation from aggressive industrial-scale campaigns that systematically extract restricted proprietary functionalities and capabilities of frontier models for the purpose of training other models. VIGIL uses this as authoritative supporting evidence for the industrial-scale, systematic-extraction and downstream-training characteristics of this class; the advisory is not treated as a generally applicable legal prohibition on distillation.

external_references.title: Stealing Machine Learning Models via Prediction APIs
external_references.evidence_note: Tramèr et al. demonstrate efficient black-box extraction attacks that use prediction API queries to duplicate deployed model functionality. This supports the systematic capability-acquisition and reproduction components of the mechanism; the experiments do not establish VIGIL's industrial-scale threshold or determine whether a particular campaign lacks an adequate authority basis.

external_references.title: NIST AI 600-1, control MS-2.10-001
external_references.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
external_references.evidence_note: EXTREQ-4FA48F69E0D84D76 identifies model extraction and reverse-engineering risk arising from outputting training samples as a red-team concern. It strongly supports systematic model-extraction and reproduction risk, but does not establish industrial scale, lack of authority, or downstream training in any particular occurrence.
